explanation: Double-quoted strings interpolate variables and recognize escape sequences like \n, while single-quoted strings treat them literally, so they are processed differently.
The null coalescing operator (??) checks like isset() and returns null silently when the operand is undefined, without emitting notices or warnings.
echo accepts multiple comma-separated arguments and prints them in order, so it outputs 'ab'.
In PHP, print always returns 1, so it can be used within expressions, e.g., $x = print 'hello'; assigns 1 to $x.
The ?: operator returns its left operand when it is truthy, and the right operand when the left is falsy.
PHP 8 changed operator precedence so that concatenation (.) now binds more loosely than addition and subtraction (e.g., 'sum: ' . $a + $b is evaluated as 'sum: ' . ($a + $b)).
The ** operator is right-associative in PHP, so 2 ** 3 ** 2 evaluates as 2 ** (3 ** 2) = 512.
In PHP 8, '.' and '+' have equal precedence and are left-associative, so ('sum: ' . 2) + 3 uses a non-numeric string in arithmetic and throws a fatal TypeError before anything is printed.
With ===, arrays must have the same key/value pairs in the same order and with identical types, so element order matters.
The == operator is a loose comparison, so 0 == false returns true; only === would return false.
PHP 8 changed string-to-number comparison, so a non-numeric string like "abc" is compared as a string and "abc" == 0 is false.
With loose comparison (==), null is cast to 0, "", and false respectively, so null == 0, null == "", and null == false are all true.
PHP casts a string to integer by taking the leading numeric portion, so '42abc' becomes 42.
PHP performs numeric type juggling, converting the string '5' to integer 5, so 5 + 5 equals 10.
In PHP, casting false to string yields an empty string "", not "0" (true becomes "1").
Due to binary floating-point representation, 0.1 + 0.2 yields a value slightly different from 0.3, so the strict comparison fails.
strrev() reverses bytes, not characters, so multibyte UTF-8 sequences become corrupted (use mb_strrev or similar instead).
str_contains() checks if the haystack contains the needle, and 'world' appears in 'Hello world', so it returns true.
str_pad() can pad on the right, left, or both sides via its optional pad_type argument (STR_PAD_RIGHT is just the default).
trim() without a character list strips whitespace including tabs, newlines, carriage returns, NUL bytes, and vertical tabs, not just spaces.
strlen counts bytes, and 'é' occupies 2 bytes in UTF-8, so 1+2+1+1+1 = 6.
A negative start parameter counts from the end of the string, so -3 returns the last three characters: 'def'.
PHP strings are immutable; ucfirst() returns a new string with the first character uppercased rather than modifying the original.
Heredoc behaves like a double-quoted string and interpolates variables, while nowdoc (quoted identifier) behaves like a single-quoted string with no parsing.
sort() reindexes the array with new numeric keys; asort() is the function that preserves key-to-value associations.
PHP automatically casts string keys containing valid decimal integers to integer keys when stored in an array.
in_array() uses loose comparison by default; strict comparison is enabled only when the third $strict parameter is set to true.
When called without a callback, array_filter() removes every element that evaluates to false (e.g., 0, "", null, false, empty array).
By default array_slice() reindexes numeric keys; keys are preserved only when the $preserve_keys parameter is set to true.
array_slice takes 2 elements starting at index 1, so it returns [20, 30].
The + union operator keeps left-side values for duplicate keys, so the result is ['a'=>1, 'b'=>2] with 2 elements.
PHP 8.1 extended array unpacking with the spread operator to support arrays with string keys.
Since PHP 8.0, named arguments can be freely mixed with spread unpacking in one call (e.g., foo(a: 1, ...$args)), with string keys in the array becoming named arguments.
In PHP, anonymous functions do not automatically capture outer-scope variables; they must be explicitly imported with the use keyword.
func_num_args() returns the number of arguments actually passed to the function at call time, regardless of the declared parameter list, so f(1, 2, 3) yields 3.
An arrow function fn must have exactly one expression as its body; statements or multiple expressions in curly braces are not allowed (use a regular closure instead).
Arrow functions capture outer variables automatically by value at definition time, not by reference at use time.
A closure declared with `static function () {}` cannot automatically capture `$this`, and `$this` cannot be bound to it later via bindTo/bind.
The variable is captured by value when the closure is created, so later changes to $x don't affect it.
In weak typing mode PHP coerces numeric strings like "5" to int automatically.
Constructor property promotion was introduced in PHP 8.0, allowing visibility and type modifiers directly on constructor parameters to declare and initialize properties.
Declaring a method as final prevents subclasses from overriding it.
The final keyword on a method prevents subclasses from overriding it, as attempting to do so causes a fatal error.
Private members of a parent class are only accessible within the class where they are declared, not in subclasses—use protected for that.
Anonymous classes are internally named 'class@anonymous' followed by a NUL byte, the file path, line number and a counter, so the part before the NUL byte is 'class@anonymous'.
Private methods are not inherited by child classes, so a same-named method in the child is treated as a brand-new declaration and may use any visibility without restriction.
__get() is also called for inaccessible properties, such as private or protected ones accessed from outside their scope.
Modifying a readonly property after initialization throws an Error (e.g., 'Cannot modify readonly property'), not an Exception.
PHP interfaces may declare constants, which are inherited by any class that implements the interface.
The instanceof operator determines whether an object is an instance of a class, an interface, or an inherited class.
PHP interfaces may declare static methods, which implementing classes must then define.
In PHP, instanceof returns true if the object is an instance of a class, a subclass, or implements a given interface.
In PHP, interface methods only declare signatures and cannot contain bodies; only traits provide method implementations.
PHP allows abstract methods to be declared public or protected (only private is forbidden), so a protected abstract method is valid.
Foo::cases() returns an array containing all cases of the enum, which are A, B, and C.
Since PHP 8.2, traits can declare constants, which must be compatible with constants in the class using the trait.
Since PHP 7, both Exception and Error implement the Throwable interface.
TypeError extends Error, not Exception; Error and Exception are separate hierarchies that only share the Throwable interface.
The @ error control operator only suppresses errors, warnings, and notices, while exceptions are still thrown and propagate normally.
Since PHP 7, intdiv() with a zero divisor throws DivisionByZeroError instead of returning false with a warning.
The finally block always executes, whether or not an exception was thrown or caught, even after uncaught exceptions or return statements.
An exception thrown in a finally block overrides and discards any pending return value (or exception) from the try block.
Any object cast to boolean in PHP evaluates to true, including instances of Exception.
register_shutdown_function() callbacks execute when script execution ends, including when exit/die is called.
The use statement only creates an alias at compile time; the class file is loaded later via autoloading when the class is actually used.
In PHP, `use function` imports a function from a namespace, while `use const` imports a constant.
PSR-4 drops the App\ prefix and maps the remaining namespace path with slashes to src/, so the file is src/Controller/Api/UserController.php.
Composer's vendor/autoload.php ultimately calls spl_autoload_register() to register its ClassLoader.
__NAMESPACE__ is a magic constant that holds the name of the current namespace (and is empty in global code).
An unqualified class name in `new` is resolved relative to the current namespace; only a leading \ makes it resolve from the global root.
PSR-4 replaces the prefix App\ with src/, so the remaining namespace Model and class User map to src/Model/User.php.

Namespace import `use` statements are only allowed at the topmost (global/namespace) scope; placing one inside a function causes a parse error, unlike closure `use` or trait `use` which are different constructs.
In PHP, arrays are value types, so assigning one array to another variable creates a copy unless you explicitly use the & reference operator.
PHP arrays are assigned by value (copy-on-write), so appending to $b doesn't affect $a, which still has 2 elements.
PHP functions have local scope, so user-defined variables from the global scope are only visible inside via the global keyword, the $GLOBALS array, or as parameters (unlike built-in superglobals).
unset($GLOBALS['x']) deletes the variable from the global scope entirely, affecting all code, not just the current function.
The parameter is passed by reference (&$x), so the increment modifies $n directly to 6.
foreach by value iterates over a copy (snapshot) of the array, so modifications made inside the loop do not affect the current iteration.
Static properties belong to the class itself and are shared across all instances, so a change made through one object is visible in all others.
PHP array keys can only be int or string; a bool key is cast to an integer (true becomes 1), so it is never stored as bool.
Since PHP 7, a generator may `return` a value, which is then retrieved by calling `getReturn()` on the Generator object after it finishes.
Once iteration of a generator has begun, calling rewind() throws an exception, so a consumed generator cannot be restarted.
Introduced in PHP 7, yield from delegates iteration to another generator, Traversable object, or array, aggregating its values.
Calling g() creates a Generator object, and get_class() returns its class name 'Generator'.
The generator yields the three values 1, 2, 3 via `yield from`, so `iterator_to_array` produces a 3-element array.
SplStack implements a LIFO (last-in, first-out) stack; SplQueue is the FIFO queue class.
ArrayIterator wraps an array (or object) and implements the Iterator interface, letting you traverse it with methods like rewind(), valid(), current(), key(), and next().
ArrayObject implements IteratorAggregate, so its elements can be traversed with foreach.
password_hash() creates a cryptographically secure salt on its own; passing a salt manually is deprecated and discouraged.
PASSWORD_DEFAULT currently points to bcrypt (PASSWORD_BCRYPT), not md5, and uses a proper adaptive hashing algorithm with an auto-generated salt.
password_verify checks 'secret' against a freshly generated valid hash of 'secret', so it returns true.
strip_tags() only removes HTML/PHP tags from a string and does nothing to neutralize SQL syntax; SQL injection requires prepared statements or proper escaping.
Calling session_regenerate_id(true) after login gives the user a new session ID, preventing attackers from fixing a known session ID.
The php_sapi_name() function returns the name of the Server API (SAPI) PHP is running under, such as 'cli' or 'fpm-fcgi'.
session_destroy() only removes session data on the server; the session cookie remains in the browser until you explicitly expire it with setcookie().
By default PHP only loads session data into $_SESSION after session_start() is called (unless session.auto_start is enabled).
array_find() was introduced in PHP 8.4 (released November 2024) via RFC to find the first element matching a callback.
PHP 8.4 introduced property hooks, allowing get/set logic to be defined directly in property declarations (e.g., public string $name { get => ...; set => ...; }).
PHP 8.4 introduced asymmetric visibility, allowing independent read and write scopes via modifiers like private(set).
The #[\NoDiscard] attribute, which marks functions whose return values should not be ignored, was introduced in PHP 8.5.
The pipe operator |> was introduced in PHP 8.5 via the 'Pipe Operator v2' RFC.
The clone-with syntax `clone($obj, ['x' => 1])` was introduced by the 'Clone with' RFC in PHP 8.5.
The array_first() and array_last() helper functions were added to PHP in version 8.5 via an accepted RFC.
The Partial Function Application v2 RFC (revised by Larry Garfield and others in 2025) was accepted targeting PHP 8.6, after the original version was declined for PHP 8.1.
The clamp_v2 RFC, adding the clamp() function, was implemented in PHP 8.5 (released in late 2025).
As of November 2026, the Context Managers RFC (including its revised v2 proposal) has not been adopted into PHP; it remained a pending/discussed proposal rather than accepted.
The Bound-Erased Generic Types (generics) RFC failed its vote and was marked as declined in 2026.
No RFC making ZTS/multithreading the default has been accepted; PHP still uses a single-threaded request execution model by default.
PHP 8.5 does not include generics; parameterized types remain an unimplemented RFC.
PHP 8.5 (GA 2025-11-20) is the latest stable version, and PHP 8.6 is scheduled to reach GA on 2026-11-19, which is after 2026-11-07.
The PHP 6 project (the Unicode experiment) was abandoned, so the version numbering skipped from PHP 5.6 straight to PHP 7.0.
The RFC for the #[\Deprecated] attribute was accepted and implemented in PHP 8.4.
In both clean and onion architecture, the dependency rule states that all dependencies point inward, so inner layers (domain/entities) have no knowledge of outer layers (UI, infrastructure).
Domain entities should be plain PHP objects decoupled from frameworks and ORMs, depending only on the language itself (and optionally the standard library).
Controllers and Twig templates belong to the presentation layer; they invoke use cases but the business logic itself resides in those use cases/services.
In onion architecture, the domain model (entities and core business logic) sits at the very center, with all other layers depending inward toward it.
Tools like deptrac analyze class dependencies against defined layer rules and fail (e.g., in CI) when a forbidden layer call is detected.

A use case should receive only plain data (DTOs/primitives) and operate through interfaces, since HTTP requests and an EntityManager are framework/infrastructure details that would couple it to the outer layers.
A Repository provides a collection-like interface for accessing aggregates/entities while hiding the underlying storage mechanism.
In clean architecture, the database is an infrastructure detail in the outer layer, so domain and use case layers remain unchanged when swapping it.
An aggregate is a cluster of domain entities and value objects treated as a single consistency unit with an aggregate root, not a database table.
A Value Object is by definition immutable and its equality is determined by the values of its attributes rather than object identity.
In Domain-Driven Design, the aggregate root is the only member of an aggregate that outside code may reference or modify, so all changes to the aggregate must pass through it.
In DDD, clients use repositories only for aggregate roots, since all other entities and objects inside the aggregate must be accessed and managed through the root.
In Domain-Driven Design, the ubiquitous language is the shared vocabulary built around the model and used consistently by both developers and domain experts.
In Domain-Driven Design, a Bounded Context is the boundary within which a model and its ubiquitous language are consistent, while the same terms outside may mean other models.
DDD advocates a rich domain model where entities and value objects encapsulate behavior; anemic models are widely considered an anti-pattern.
A bounded context defines an explicit boundary where a single model applies, so concepts like Order or Shipment exist as separate classes per context with only the attributes/behavior relevant there.
Symfony's container only instantiates a service when it is first requested or injected, not when the container is compiled or booted.
The Symfony console command `debug:router` (run as `php bin/console debug:router`) displays all registered routes.
Symfony autowiring automatically injects dependencies and autoconfigures services, so manual declaration of every service in services.yaml is not required.
Twig compiles templates into optimized PHP classes that are stored in a cache and reused across requests instead of being recompiled.
Symfony caches the compiled container in the dev environment and recompiles it only when one of its tracked resources (config files, classes, env vars, etc.) changes.
Symfony uses the APP_ENV environment variable (set in .env) to select the active environment, e.g. dev or prod.
Symfony only routes to public methods (or __invoke), since it calls the controller from outside the class, so a private method cannot be used as a controller action.
Subscribers and listeners are dispatched in the same order based on their priority value (0 by default); implementing EventSubscriberInterface confers no automatic priority.
Symfony 6.0 removed the deprecated Guard authenticator system, so authentication is now built exclusively on AuthenticatorInterface-based authenticators.
The #[IsGranted('ROLE_ADMIN')] attribute on a controller method throws AccessDeniedException (HTTP 403) when the user lacks the required role/permission.
Symfony voters implement the Voter interface to decide if the current user can perform an action (attribute) on a specific object (subject), checked via isGranted('EDIT', $post).
Symfony 7 dropped support for Doctrine annotations, so validation constraints must be declared as PHP native attributes like #[Assert\NotBlank].
Symfony forms enable CSRF protection by default, automatically adding and validating the _token field on submission.
Symfony validation always executes on the server using constraint definitions, regardless of any client-side HTML5 validation results.
The Symfony MakerBundle command make:form generates a form type class (FormType).
Symfony never stores the plain-text password in the session; it only stores a hash-based password signature used to detect password changes.
Symfony stores each bundle's configuration as a separate YAML (or PHP) file under config/packages, such as framework.yaml, twig.yaml, or doctrine.yaml.
This is the standard dotenv practice (e.g., in Symfony): the committed .env holds safe defaults, while .env.local contains local secrets and is excluded from version control.
The `php bin/console debug:container` command lists all registered services and their aliases in the dependency injection container.
By the time a controller runs, the container is frozen/compiled, so calling setParameter() throws an exception; parameters must be set during the compile phase, e.g. in a compiler pass or Extension.
Since Symfony 3.4/4.0, services are private by default (public: false), so they must be injected via dependency injection rather than fetched directly from the container.
Many bundles work out of the box with sensible defaults, so a config/packages file is optional, not mandatory.
In Symfony, environment variables are injected into services.yaml parameters and arguments using the %env(VAR)% syntax.
In Symfony, setting APP_DEBUG=1 (in .env or the environment) enables debug mode, which activates the web profiler and Twig debugging.
Symfony Messenger allows a message to be handled by multiple handlers, all of which are executed when the message is dispatched.
The sync transport handles messages immediately in the same process without queuing, unlike async which queues them for a worker.
The Symfony command `php bin/console messenger:consume` starts the worker that pulls and processes messages from the transport queues.
In Symfony Messenger, the retry_strategy options (max_retries, delay, multiplier, etc.) are defined individually under each transport's configuration.
Symfony Messenger's default serializer encodes message bodies as JSON (with headers carrying the message type), so messages are serialized to JSON by default.
The Scheduler component (Symfony 6.2+) produces messages according to a schedule and relies on Messenger transports to dispatch and consume them.
Symfony Messenger's built-in doctrine transport (used as doctrine://...) persists queued messages in database tables managed by Doctrine.
Symfony Messenger allows adding custom middleware services (via tagging or configuration) and ordering them before or after the built-in middleware in the bus stack.
Symfony's official release process states that major versions are released every two years and minor versions every six months, in May and November.
Symfony 8 requires PHP 8.4 or higher, following Symfony's pattern of raising the minimum PHP version with each major release.
Symfony 7.0 removed support for docblock annotations (e.g. for validation and routes); only native PHP attributes are supported.
Symfony's AssetMapper serves and versions CSS/JS directly, using importmap.php for JS module imports, with no Node.js or webpack required.
Symfony 6.4 (released November 2023) is an LTS release supported with bug fixes and security patches until 2027.
In Symfony, deprecations only keep working within a major branch; when a new major version is released, all deprecated features of the previous branch are removed.
Symfony publishes an UPGRADE guide (e.g., UPGRADE-6.0.md) with every major release documenting the changes and backward compatibility breaks.
Symfony's AssetMapper component serves and versioned-manages assets and handles JavaScript importmaps natively, without requiring Node.js or webpack.
Symfony 8.2 is scheduled for release in late November 2026, so it had not yet been released as of 2026-11-07.
Symfony 8.0 was released in November 2025, so following the six-month release cycle, 8.1 came in May 2026 and 8.2 is scheduled for November 2026.
Symfony follows a 6-month minor release cycle, so the version after 8.1 (May 2026) is 8.2 (November 2026).
An x.2 release is a minor release that maintains backward compatibility, so applications do not need to be rewritten; only major versions introduce breaking changes.
PHP guarantees backward compatibility only between patch releases (e.g., 8.1.5 → 8.1.6); minor releases like 8.1 → 8.2 can introduce backward-incompatible changes.
Symfony releases the final minor version of a major branch as its LTS (following the x.4 pattern, like 6.4), so the last 8.x release before Symfony 9.0 is 8.4.
Symfony only raises its minimum PHP requirement in major releases (x.0), so a minor release like 8.2 cannot introduce a new PHP requirement such as 8.5.
Symfony's policy keeps deprecations added in a minor version (8.x) in place until the next major version (9.0), where they are removed.
Twig is sandboxed by design; inside {{ }} you can only use registered functions, filters, and allowed methods, not arbitrary PHP code.
Twig enables auto-escaping with the 'html' strategy by default, so printed variables are escaped unless disabled.
The |e filter escapes a string using the html strategy by default, making it safe to output in an HTML context.
The format_number filter from twig/intl-extra uses PHP's NumberFormatter to format a number according to the given locale.
In Twig, the |raw filter marks a value as safe, so auto-escaping is not applied to it.
In Twig, {{ }} echoes an expression's value, while {% %} contains logic tags like if, for, and set.
Twig provides the `{% set %}` tag to declare and assign variables directly within a template.
Twig provides the dump() function to output the debug structure of a variable (requires the debug extension/environment).
Bootstrap provides prebuilt CSS and JavaScript UI components (grids, buttons, modals), whereas SPA frameworks like Angular, React, or Vue manage application architecture.
The .container class is responsive and applies a fixed max-width at each breakpoint, unlike .container-fluid which is always full-width.
Bootstrap's grid (when float-based) uses 12 columns, not 16.
Bootstrap 5 defines six breakpoints, but xs has no infix, so the five infixes used in class names are sm, md, lg, xl, and xxl.
In Bootstrap, spacing utilities like .mt-3 or .px-2 are generated as multiples of the $spacer variable (defaulting to 1rem).
Bootstrap 5 uses the data-bs-toggle attribute (e.g. data-bs-toggle="dropdown") to enable interactive components on an element.
Bootstrap 5 removed the jQuery dependency, so all components can be initialized and controlled with plain vanilla JavaScript.
Bootstrap 5.3 dark mode is enabled with the data-bs-theme="dark" attribute on the root element, not a .dark class.
Doctrine ORM only maps entities to existing tables; schema must be created beforehand with tools like SchemaTool or migrations, not automatically at runtime.
EntityManager::persist() tells Doctrine to manage a new entity, with any INSERT deferred until flush() is called.
Doctrine ORM 3 removed EntityManager::merge(); detached entities can no longer be merged via the EntityManager.
DQL is Doctrine's object-oriented query language that operates on entities, associations, and fields, which Doctrine then translates into SQL over tables and columns.
Doctrine's Repository::find() returns null when no entity matches the given identifier.
DoctrineBundle does not auto-flush; you must call flush() explicitly, it only closes the connection after the response.
Once an entity is managed, Doctrine's Unit of Work detects changes automatically and flush() persists them without needing persist() again.
In Doctrine ORM, remove() only marks an entity for deletion; the actual DELETE query is executed when flush() is called.
MVCC in PostgreSQL ensures readers do not block writers and writers do not block readers by maintaining multiple row versions.
The EXPLAIN command displays the query execution plan (e.g., join types, indexes used) without actually running the query.

IDENTITY is the SQL-standard mechanism with GENERATED ALWAYS/BY DEFAULT semantics that restricts explicit value insertion and alteration, while SERIAL is a legacy shorthand that merely sets a nextval() default and imposes no such restrictions.
PostgreSQL by default treats NULLs as distinct from each other, so a UNIQUE constraint permits multiple rows with NULL (unless NULLS NOT DISTINCT is specified).
PostgreSQL's string_agg(value, separator) aggregate function concatenates string values from multiple rows using a delimiter.
Plain VACUUM only marks dead tuple space as reusable within the table; only VACUUM FULL, which rewrites the table, returns space to the operating system.
In a window function's OVER() clause, the PARTITION BY keyword splits rows into groups over which the function is computed.
READ COMMITTED only prevents dirty reads; non-repeatable reads (and phantom reads) can still occur at this level.
PostgreSQL executes each standalone SQL statement inside its own implicit transaction and commits it automatically unless a transaction is explicitly started.
The COMMIT command ends a transaction and permanently saves all its changes.
Indexes speed up any WHERE-clause row lookup, so UPDATE and DELETE statements that search on an indexed column find rows faster, just like SELECT.
PostgreSQL supports SAVEPOINT, which lets you roll back part of a transaction with ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT without aborting the whole transaction.
EXPLAIN ANALYZE actually executes the query to show real execution statistics; plain EXPLAIN shows the plan without running it.
The pgvector extension adds a vector data type, distance operators, and index types (IVFFlat/HNSW) for similarity search over embeddings in PostgreSQL.
A partial index includes only the rows for which its WHERE predicate evaluates to true.
PostgreSQL implements SERIALIZABLE using Serializable Snapshot Isolation (SSI), which detects serialization conflicts rather than locking read rows.
HTTP 201 is the 'Created' status code, indicating the request successfully resulted in a new resource.
HTTP 204 (No Content) indicates a successful request where the response body is empty, commonly used after DELETE.
Per RFC 7231/9110, DELETE is defined as idempotent—repeating the same DELETE request leaves the resource in the same (deleted) state.
Access-Control-Allow-Origin is sent by the server in its response to indicate which origins it permits, not by the client.
HTTP 429 Too Many Requests indicates the client has sent too many requests in a given time period, i.e., exceeded a rate limit.
It's reversed: 4xx codes indicate client errors (e.g., 404) and 5xx codes indicate server-side errors (e.g., 500).
The Content-Type header describes the MIME type of the request or response body.
RFC 5789 explicitly states PATCH is neither safe nor idempotent, while PUT is required to be idempotent.
Plain == is vulnerable to timing attacks; use password_verify() or hash_equals() for timing-safe comparison.
CSRF tokens are generated server-side, tied to the user's session, included in forms, and validated server-side on unsafe (state-changing) requests to reject forged requests.
The standard HTTP header used to enable a Content Security Policy is "Content-Security-Policy" (the old X-Content-Security-Policy and X-WebKit-CSP headers are deprecated).
OAuth 2.0 is an authorization (delegation) framework; an access token grants scopes to a client and does not identify the user, which is why OpenID Connect was built on top of it for authentication.
XSS is prevented by escaping/output-encoding data when it is sent to the browser, not by input validation before storing it.
In the authorization code flow, the authorization server returns an authorization code (parameter 'code') to the redirect_uri, which the client then exchanges for an access token.
In OAuth 2.0, refresh tokens are long-lived credentials issued alongside short-lived access tokens, enabling new access tokens to be obtained without user re-authentication.
Salts are not secrets; they are stored alongside the hash and merely need to be available (not confidential) to recompute and verify the hash.
For PHPUnit to recognize and run test methods, the class must extend (or use, e.g. abstract bases ultimately derived from) PHPUnit\Framework\TestCase.
setUp() runs before each test method; setUpBeforeClass() is the method that runs once before all tests in the class.
A PHPUnit data provider supplies multiple sets of arguments, so the test runs once for each data set it returns.
PHPUnit's expectException(string $exception) method sets the expectation that a test will throw an exception of the given class.
It's reversed: a stub only returns configured values, while a mock also verifies that expected methods were called.
PHPUnit 10 introduced native metadata attributes such as #[DataProvider], deprecating the old @dataProvider doc-comment annotation, which was removed in PHPUnit 12.
PHPUnit supports test dependencies via the @depends annotation, where a test can receive the return value of the test it depends on.
PHPUnit runs tests in random order when invoked with the --order-by=random option.
